zebralogic.title: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue uses terms like “directly left of”, “directly right of”, or “next to”, enforce that the two houses are adjacent and respect the indicated direction; for non‑adjacent ordering terms like “somewhere left of”, enforce only a strict inequality.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue contains adjacency or ordering language.
zebralogic.example: Treating “Peter is directly left of the Victorian house” as allowing Peter to be any house left of the Victorian house, rather than the immediate neighbor.

zebralogic.title: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality
zebralogic.principle: Clues that say “somewhere left of” or “somewhere right of” impose only a strict ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y) or >) without requiring adjacency.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains the phrase “somewhere left/right of”.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting “the tall house is somewhere left of the garden house” as requiring the two houses to be adjacent.

zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; duplicate assignments violate the puzzle constraints.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After applying all clues, verify that every attribute value is used exactly once.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the house style “ranch” to two different houses.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: Copy attribute values verbatim as they appear in the problem statement, preserving spelling and case, because the verifier matches them exactly.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When constructing the final JSON output.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for name‑attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: If a clue links a specific name to an attribute (e.g., “Alice is tall”), enforce both directions: the named person must have that attribute, and that attribute must belong to that person.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue directly ties a name to a value.
zebralogic.example: Allowing Alice to be tall while also letting another person be tall.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for attribute‑attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue states that two non‑name attributes belong to the same house (e.g., “the craftsman house has average height”), enforce that they co‑occur and that each implies the other.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue links two attribute values.
zebralogic.example: Placing average height in a house but giving that house a different style than craftsman.

zebralogic.title: Apply direct placement constraints
zebralogic.principle: If a clue explicitly places an attribute in a specific house number (e.g., “the Victorian house is house 5”), enforce that exact placement and propagate all related constraints from it.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains a specific house index.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring “the Victorian house is house 5” and allowing a Victorian house elsewhere.

zebralogic.title: Output solution JSON with exact schema and no extra text
zebralogic.principle: Emit only the JSON object with top‑level keys “reasoning” and “solution” and the required table; any extra characters cause the verifier to reject the answer.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: At the very end of the response.
zebralogic.example: Adding explanatory sentences before the JSON object.

zebralogic.title: Chain adjacency clues into consecutive blocks
zebralogic.principle: When multiple adjacency clues share a common intermediate attribute (e.g., A left of B and B left of C), combine them into a block to enforce the full order and reduce search space.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When adjacency clues form a chain.
zebralogic.example: Treating “A left of B” and “B left of C” independently, leading to contradictory placements.

zebralogic.title: Consistent target in multiple adjacency clues
zebralogic.principle: If several adjacency clues refer to the same target attribute (e.g., “X is directly left of the high‑school house” and “Y is directly left of the high‑school house”), enforce that X and Y must be the same house, because there is only one target house.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When processing adjacency clues that share the same right‑hand side attribute.
zebralogic.example: Placing the “short” person left of the high‑school house and the “knitting” person left of the high‑school house in different houses.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model confuses the phrasing of separation clues, treating them as a simple distance rather than the required number of houses in between.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Parse “N houses between X and Y” as exactly N other houses separating X and Y, not as a distance of N houses.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats each clue in isolation and fails to enforce that linked attributes must co‑occur.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Whenever a clue states two attributes belong together, add a bidirectional constraint linking them.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The solver may assign the same value to multiple houses when focusing on satisfying individual clues.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: After each assignment, check that every attribute value appears exactly once; reject any duplicate.

zebralogic.description: Altering attribute values (spelling/casing) instead of copying them verbatim
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalises text for readability, forgetting that the verifier requires exact matches.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute strings exactly as given, preserving case and spelling.

zebralogic.description: Including extra explanatory text or stray characters outside the required JSON solution
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model tries to be helpful by adding commentary, which interferes with the strict parser.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Output only the JSON object with the prescribed keys and no surrounding text.

zebralogic.description: Misinterpreting adjacency clues (e.g., treating “directly left of” as non‑adjacent or ignoring direction)
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model conflates adjacency with general ordering, losing the requirement that the houses be immediate neighbors.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Distinguish “directly left/right of” (adjacent) from “somewhere left/right of” (inequality) and enforce the correct relationship.
